bibl.title: Using Deep Learning for Image-Based Plant Disease Detection

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: 54,306 leaf images spanning 38 crop-disease classes, 14 crop species and 26 diseases
span.quote: At the outset, we note that on a dataset with 38 class labels, random guessing will only achieve an overall accuracy of 2.63% on average.

span.label: whether a deep convolutional network can identify crop species and disease from a leaf image without hand-engineered features - and the dataset to do it on, which did not exist
span.quote: In order to develop accurate image classifiers for the purposes of plant disease diagnosis, we needed a large, verified dataset of images of diseased and healthy plants. Until very recently, such a dataset did not exist, and even smaller datasets were not freely available.

span.label: 99.35% on a held-out split, and - reported in the same paper - 31.40% on images drawn from other sources
span.quote: Using the best model on these datasets, we obtained an overall accuracy of 31.40% in dataset 1, and 31.69% in dataset 2, in successfully predicting the correct class label (i.e., crop and disease information) from among 38 possible class labels. We note that a random classifier will obtain an average accuracy of only 2.63%.

span.label: method
span.quote: Here, we demonstrate the technical feasibility using a deep learning approach utilizing 54,306 images of 14 crop species with 26 diseases (or healthy) made openly available through the project PlantVillage (Hughes and Salathé, 2015 ).

span.label: identification of crop disease from a photograph of a leaf
span.quote: The trained model achieves an accuracy of 99.35% on a held-out test set, demonstrating the feasibility of this approach.

span.label: AlexNet and GoogLeNet trained both from scratch and by transfer learning, across colour, gray-scale and segmented copies and five train/test splits
span.term: AlexNet and GoogLeNet trained both from scratch and by transfer learning, across colour, gray-scale and segmented copies and five train/test splits
span.quote: In other words, the key difference between these two learning approaches (transfer vs. training from scratch) is in the initial state of weights of a few layers, which lets the transfer learning approach exploit the large amount of visual knowledge already learned by the pre-trained AlexNet and GoogleNet models extracted from ImageNet (Russakovsky et al., 2015 ).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: TRANSFER LEARNING AS RE-USED VISUAL KNOWLEDGE: only the initial weights of a few layers differ, which lets the model exploit what the pre-trained network already learned from ImageNet
span.quote: In other words, the key difference between these two learning approaches (transfer vs. training from scratch) is in the initial state of weights of a few layers, which lets the transfer learning approach exploit the large amount of visual knowledge already learned by the pre-trained AlexNet and GoogleNet models extracted from ImageNet (Russakovsky et al., 2015 ).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: WHY THE HAND-ENGINEERED PIPELINE DOES NOT SCALE: performance depends on predefined features, so the feature-design step has to be redone whenever the problem or the dataset changes
span.quote: Previously, the traditional approach for image classification tasks has been based on hand-engineered features, such as SIFT (Lowe, 2004 ), HoG (Dalal and Triggs, 2005 ), SURF (Bay et al., 2008 ), etc., and then to use some form of learning algorithm in these feature spaces. The performance of these approaches thus depended heavily on the underlying predefined features. Feature engineering itself is a complex and tedious process which needs to be revisited every time the problem at hand or the associated dataset changes considerably.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: THE COST IS ALL IN TRAINING, NOT IN USE: hours on a GPU cluster to train, under a second on a CPU to classify - which is what makes a phone the deployment target
span.quote: Importantly, while the training of the model takes a lot of time (multiple hours on a high performance GPU cluster computer), the classification itself is very fast (less than a second on a CPU), and can thus easily be implemented on a smartphone.

span.label: Accuracy falls from 99.35% to just above 31% when the test images come from somewhere other than the dataset the model was trained on - the paper's own headline number does not survive the change of source
span.quote: First, when tested on a set of images taken under conditions different from the images used for training, the model's accuracy is reduced substantially, to just above 31%. It's important to note that this accuracy is much higher than the one based on random selection of 38 classes (2.6%), but nevertheless, a more diverse set of training data is needed to improve the accuracy.

span.label: The model is trained and tested on SINGLE LEAVES, FACING UP, ON A HOMOGENEOUS BACKGROUND, while many diseases do not present on the upper side of a leaf at all
span.quote: The second limitation is that we are currently constrained to the classification of single leaves, facing up, on a homogeneous background. While these are straightforward conditions, a real world application should be able to classify images of a disease as it presents itself directly on the plant. Indeed, many diseases don't present themselves on the upper side of leaves only (or at all), but on many different parts of the plant.

span.label: The 38-class task is harder than the real one: growers know which crop they planted, so requiring the model to identify the crop as well inflates the difficulty
span.quote: At the same time, by using 38 classes that contain both crop species and disease status, we have made the challenge harder than ultimately necessary from a practical perspective, as growers are expected to know which crops they are growing.

span.label: Offered as a supplement to laboratory diagnosis and not a replacement, on the paper's own statement that lab tests are always more reliable than visual symptoms
span.quote: Finally, it's worth noting that the approach presented here is not intended to replace existing solutions for disease diagnosis, but rather to supplement them. Laboratory tests are ultimately always more reliable than diagnoses based on visual symptoms alone, and oftentimes early-stage diagnosis via visual inspection alone is challenging.

span.label: the whole experiment re-run on GRAY-SCALED and SEGMENTED copies of the same images
span.note: eliminates: whether the network learned plant disease or learned the dataset's own collection biases
span.quote: This set of experiments was designed to understand if the neural network actually learns the “notion” of plant diseases, or if it is just learning the inherent biases in the dataset.

span.label: the background removed by segmentation, so the regularised collection process cannot carry the signal
span.note: eliminates: background as a confound in a controlled-capture dataset
span.quote: finally we run all the experiments on a version of the PlantVillage dataset where the leaves were segmented, hence removing all the extra background information which might have the potential to introduce some inherent bias in the dataset due to the regularized process of data collection in case of PlantVillage dataset.

span.label: the train/test split pushed to the extreme of 20% train and 80% test
span.note: eliminates: over-fitting to the training split
span.quote: To address the issue of over-fitting, we vary the test set to train set ratio and observe that even in the extreme case of training on only 20% of the data and testing the trained model on the rest 80% of the data, the model achieves an overall accuracy of 98.21% (mean F 1 score of 0.9820) in the case of GoogLeNet::TransferLearning::Color::20–80 . As expected, the overall performance of both AlexNet and GoogLeNet do degrade if we keep increasing the test set to train set ratio (see Figure 3D ), but the decrease in performance is not as drastic as we would expect if the model was indeed over-fitting.

span.label: validation loss and training loss checked for divergence
span.note: eliminates: over-fitting, and the check came back negative
span.quote: Figure 3C also shows that there is no divergence between the validation loss and the training loss, confirming that over-fitting is not a contributor to the results we obtain across all our experiments.

span.label: transfer learning
span.quote: In other words, the key difference between these two learning approaches (transfer vs. training from scratch) is in the initial state of weights of a few layers, which lets the transfer learning approach exploit the large amount of visual knowledge already learned by the pre-trained AlexNet and GoogleNet models extracted from ImageNet (Russakovsky et al., 2015 ).

span.label: training from scratch

span.label: AlexNet
span.quote: Among the AlexNet and GoogLeNet architectures, GoogLeNet consistently performs better than AlexNet (Figure 3A ), and based on the method of training, transfer learning always yields better results (Figure 3B ), both of which were expected.

span.label: GoogLeNet
span.quote: Among the AlexNet and GoogLeNet architectures, GoogLeNet consistently performs better than AlexNet (Figure 3A ), and based on the method of training, transfer learning always yields better results (Figure 3B ), both of which were expected.

span.label: over-fitting
span.quote: Figure 3C also shows that there is no divergence between the validation loss and the training loss, confirming that over-fitting is not a contributor to the results we obtain across all our experiments.

span.label: feature engineering
span.quote: The absence of the labor-intensive phase of feature engineering and the generalizability of the solution makes them a very promising candidate for a practical and scaleable approach for computational inference of plant diseases.

span.label: hand-engineered features
span.quote: Previously, the traditional approach for image classification tasks has been based on hand-engineered features, such as SIFT (Lowe, 2004 ), HoG (Dalal and Triggs, 2005 ), SURF (Bay et al., 2008 ), etc., and then to use some form of learning algorithm in these feature spaces. The performance of these approaches thus depended heavily on the underlying predefined features. Feature engineering itself is a complex and tedious process which needs to be revisited every time the problem at hand or the associated dataset changes considerably.

span.label: traditional approach
span.quote: Previously, the traditional approach for image classification tasks has been based on hand-engineered features, such as SIFT (Lowe, 2004 ), HoG (Dalal and Triggs, 2005 ), SURF (Bay et al., 2008 ), etc., and then to use some form of learning algorithm in these feature spaces. The performance of these approaches thus depended heavily on the underlying predefined features. Feature engineering itself is a complex and tedious process which needs to be revisited every time the problem at hand or the associated dataset changes considerably.

span.label: inherent biases
span.quote: This set of experiments was designed to understand if the neural network actually learns the “notion” of plant diseases, or if it is just learning the inherent biases in the dataset.

span.label: background information
span.quote: finally we run all the experiments on a version of the PlantVillage dataset where the leaves were segmented, hence removing all the extra background information which might have the potential to introduce some inherent bias in the dataset due to the regularized process of data collection in case of PlantVillage dataset.

It's important to note that this accuracy is much higher than the one based on random selection of 38 classes (2.6%), but nevertheless, a more diverse set of training data is needed to improve the accuracy.
